previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a male with a history of HLA-B27-positive ankylosing spondylitis, hypertension, asthma, obstructive sleep apnea, and anxiety, was admitted for acute worsening of chronic right-sided back, flank, and rib pain over three weeks, along with new-onset severe nausea, vomiting, and early satiety. Pain was managed with IV and oral hydromorphone, and the pain service performed trigger point injections, leading to moderate improvement. Labs showed mild inflammation with CRP of 11 and no evidence of infection, organ dysfunction, or metabolic disturbance. Nausea was not clearly linked to medications or H. pylori and may be related to pain or functional gastrointestinal issues. The patient was transitioned back to his home regimen of oral Dilaudid, omeprazole, and other chronic medications. He was discharged home after three days with stable pain, improved nausea, and plans to follow up in pain clinic and with his PCP for further evaluation of early satiety, possibly including an outpatient endoscopy.

Brief Hospital Course:
Mr. ___ is a ___ M with HLA B27 positive ankylosing 
spondylitis (diagnosed in ___ who presented on the evening of 
___ with 1 week history of worsening mid/upper back pain. He is 
followed by chronic pain and receives trigger point injections. 
His primary care doctor prescribes his opiate pain medications.

The patient was admitted to the general medicine service and 
treated for his pain. Labs on admission notable for elevated 
ESR/CRP (which might be explained by his underlying ankylosing 
spondylitis), no leukocytosis. Patient declined consultation 
with chronic pain. Because his pain was not lower back that is 
typical of his flares, an X-ray of his cervical and thoracic 
spine was obtained to evaluate for fracture. There was no 
fracture. 

Of note, the patient reported a fever of 102 several days before 
coming to be evaluated. He was afebrile during his 
hospitalization. The differential of back pain with elevated 
inflammatory markers, fevers does include discitis. If pain 
worsens or patient has recurrent fevers, CT or MR should be 
pursued. It was emphasized to the patient he should report 
fevers of >100 degrees, worsening back pain to his primary care 
physician.
